title: How to Automate Gmail Attachment Intake and Extraction with Jinba
summary: Jinba turns Gmail attachments into structured intake records: scheduled polling, extract fields via Reducto, validate rules, log to Sheets or Snowflake, route to a human reviewer.
body_markdown:
### Summary


- Incoming intake emails still require manual opening, reading, extraction, rule checking, logging, and assignment, creating time loss and compounding errors.
- Attachments arrive as scanned PDFs, digital forms, and formatted spreadsheets, so template-only extraction breaks when layouts shift.
- The four-step workflow is: poll Gmail on a schedule for new messages, extract fields with Document Processing and Reducto, validate with Modules Checker V2, then route to Google Sheets or Snowflake for human review.
- Validation keeps malformed records out of the structured log; important because up to 80% of enterprise data remains underutilised due to inefficient data management.
- Human approval remains mandatory, and teams can deploy this intake workflow with[Jinba Flow](https://flow.jinba.io/) before testing each step against real document samples.


Claims, compliance, and legal intake teams receive a continuous stream of emails with attached documents: claim forms, policy submissions, legal notices, invoices. Each message requires manual opening, reading, extraction of relevant fields, validation against business rules, logging, and assignment to the correct team. That sequence takes time at every step, and the error rate compounds across volume.


The specific friction points are consistent. Incoming attachments arrive in mixed formats. Intake queues receive scanned PDFs, digitally generated forms, and formatted spreadsheets, all carrying the same fields but in different positions and layouts. Manual re-keying introduces errors, and without a structured log there is no reliable audit trail when a regulator or senior reviewer asks what happened to a specific submission.


This guide covers a four-step Gmail workflow built on[Jinba](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/communication/gmail) : trigger on arrival, extract fields from attachments, validate against business rules, then route to a structured log and a human reviewer. No step sends data or communications autonomously.


## Step 1: Poll for New Messages on a Schedule with the Gmail Tool


The workflow starts with Jinba's[Gmail tool](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/communication/gmail) , which connects directly to the[Gmail API](https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/guides) . The Gmail tool is a polling/CRUD tool with no event trigger, so the workflow runs on a schedule. On each run, the` GMAIL_LIST_MESSAGES` action lists the messages in a specified Gmail account that meet defined criteria — a matching label, a sender domain, a subject line pattern, or the presence of an attachment — and` GMAIL_GET_MESSAGE` fetches the full message for any new arrival.


Because the tool polls on a schedule rather than receiving push notifications, the workflow processes new messages on the next scheduled run after they arrive. This removes the need for someone to watch the inbox manually.


Configuration at this stage should be specific. Intake teams typically monitor a dedicated address such asclaims@company.com or apply a Gmail label such as` Intake - Legal` to route qualifying messages before the workflow lists them. The Gmail API's[filter settings](https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/guides/filter%5Fsettings) support automated labelling rules, so teams can pre-sort incoming mail by sender or subject before the workflow receives it.[Labels](https://developers.google.com/workspace/gmail/api/guides/labels) can also be applied programmatically as the workflow proceeds, giving teams a live view of processing status directly inside Gmail.


The listing step passes the full message metadata and attachment references downstream. Nothing is extracted or acted on yet.


## Step 2: Extract Fields with Document Processing and Reducto


Once the trigger fires, Jinba pulls the attachments and passes them to the extraction layer. Two tools handle this:[Document Processing](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/files/document%5Fprocessing) and[Reducto](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/files/reducto) .


Document Processing applies OCR and parses documents into plain text. Named-field extraction is handled by Reducto (` REDUCTO_EXTRACT` ), a separate tool that handles more complex or unstructured layouts, including scanned documents with irregular formatting or non-standard templates. This combination reduces sensitivity to layout variation, the common failure point for template-based extractors: when the layout shifts, rigid templates break.


In practice, intake teams define the fields they need at configuration time. For a claims workflow, those fields include:


- ` Claimant_Name`
- ` Policy_Number`
- ` Date_of_Incident`
- ` Claim_Type`
- ` Supporting_Document_Count`
- ` Invoice_Total`


Jinba locates each field in the attachment and returns a structured data object. When a message contains multiple attachments, each is processed in sequence and the results are held together under the originating message reference.


This step addresses the operational difficulty of document automation at scale: the diversity of incoming file types and binary data. Legal and compliance intake queues rarely receive documents in a single consistent format. The extraction layer handles that variation so downstream steps receive clean, consistently structured data regardless of the original submission format.


## Step 3: Validate with Jinba Modules Checker V2


Extracted data is not necessarily correct data. A field can be present and still fail a business rule: a policy number in the wrong format, a date outside the valid range, a required field that OCR returned as blank because the submitter left it empty.


[Jinba Modules Checker V2](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/validation/jinba%5Fmodules%5Fchecker%5Fv2) applies rule-based validation to the extracted data object before anything is logged or routed. Intake teams define the rules at configuration time. Representative examples:


- ` Policy_Number` must match the pattern` POL-XXXXXXX`
- ` Date_of_Incident` must be a valid date and must not be in the future
- ` Claimant_Name` must not be empty
- ` Invoice_Total` must be a positive numeric value


Documents that pass all rules continue downstream. Documents that fail are flagged and held for manual review, with the specific rule failures recorded alongside the extracted data. This means reviewers see not just that a document failed, but which field failed and why, which is the information they need to resolve it.


Validation at this stage keeps bad data out of the structured log. For compliance teams, this matters because[up to 80% of enterprise data remains underutilised due to inefficient data management](https://www.forbes.com/councils/forbestechcouncil/2024/05/29/businesses-have-invested-deeply-in-data-but-theyre-still-just-scratching-the-surface/) . A log full of incomplete or malformed records compounds the problem rather than solving it.


## Step 4: Route, Log, and Assign for Human Review


Validated records are routed to one or both of two destinations:[Google Sheets](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/productivity/google%5Fsheets) or Snowflake. Each validated document creates a new row or record containing all extracted fields, the originating message ID, the timestamp of receipt, and the validation outcome. This log is the primary audit record for the intake workflow.


Google Sheets is appropriate for teams that need immediate, shareable visibility without a data warehouse dependency. Snowflake is appropriate for teams that feed intake data into broader analytics pipelines or require long-term structured storage at volume.


Routing logic can branch on document attributes. A high-value claim above a defined threshold routes to a senior reviewer. A document from a specific sender domain routes to the team responsible for that account. A failed validation routes to a triage queue rather than the standard assignment pool.


### Human review is not optional


Jinba does not send communications or finalise records autonomously. When the workflow generates a draft response, such as an acknowledgement to the submitter, that draft appears as a card in the assigned reviewer's queue. The reviewer reads it, edits it if needed, and approves it before it is sent.


This is the[human-in-the-loop](https://www.databricks.com/blog/human-in-the-loop) model applied at the point where the risk is highest. For claims, compliance, and legal teams, the consequences of an incorrect or premature communication are material. A policy number transposed in an acknowledgement letter, or a response sent to the wrong party, creates liability. The draft card mechanism means a human has reviewed every outbound action before it occurs. The system handles extraction, structuring, and drafting. The human handles approval.


This distinction also answers the accountability problem that consistently undermines AI projects in regulated environments. Clear ownership of each action in the workflow, with a named reviewer attached to every approval event, makes the process auditable and defensible.


## The Audit Trail


Every document that passes through this workflow generates a log entry that covers:


- The timestamp the email was received
- The sender and subject of the originating message
- The names and types of attachments processed
- The fields extracted and their values
- The validation result for each rule applied
- The assigned reviewer and the time of assignment
- The review outcome and any edits made before approval


This record is written at each step as the workflow executes, not reconstructed after the fact. For a regulatory review or an internal audit, the log answers questions about any specific document without requiring anyone to reconstruct what happened from memory or email history.


Legal and compliance workflows have always required this kind of accountability. The automation does not change that requirement. It makes the record more complete and more consistent than a manual process typically produces.


## What to Do Next


The workflow described here covers a complete intake path from Gmail trigger to structured log and human-reviewed output. Teams configuring a new workflow should configure the Gmail trigger first, test it against a sample of real incoming documents, and confirm that the extraction layer returns the expected fields before enabling the validation and routing steps.


The[Jinba Gmail documentation](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/communication/gmail) is the starting point for listing configuration, including the scheduled run and label-based filtering. The[Document Processing](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/files/document%5Fprocessing) and[Reducto](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/files/reducto) documentation covers field definition and extraction configuration. The[Modules Checker V2 reference](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/validation/jinba%5Fmodules%5Fchecker%5Fv2) covers rule syntax and failure handling. The[Google Sheets integration](https://docs.jinba.io/en/pages/tools/productivity/google%5Fsheets) covers log structure and row mapping.


Build and test each step in sequence rather than activating the full workflow at once. Incremental testing against realistic document samples closes the gap between a proof of concept and a production-ready intake process.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is Jinba, and how does it automate Gmail document intake?


Jinba is an automation platform that connects Gmail to document extraction, validation, and routing tools. It triggers when an email with attachments arrives, extracts structured data from the attachments, validates that data against business rules, and routes the result to a spreadsheet, data warehouse, or human review queue.


### How does the Jinba Gmail workflow trigger when a new email arrives?


Jinba runs the workflow on a schedule and uses the` GMAIL_LIST_MESSAGES` action to poll the inbox for new emails, with` GMAIL_GET_MESSAGE` fetching the full message. Operators configure the listing to match a dedicated intake address, label, sender domain, or subject line pattern, so the workflow processes qualifying messages on each scheduled run.


### What types of attachments can Jinba extract data from?


Jinba can process scanned PDFs, digitally generated forms, and formatted spreadsheets. The workflow combines Document Processing for OCR and plain-text parsing with Reducto (` REDUCTO_EXTRACT` ) for named-field extraction and complex or irregular layouts, so the same intake pipeline works even when incoming attachments use different formats and templates.


### How does Jinba validate extracted data from claims, compliance, or legal documents?


Jinba Modules Checker V2 applies configurable business rules to each extracted field. For example, it can require a policy number to match a specific pattern, reject future incident dates, or flag an empty claimant name. Documents that fail validation are held for manual review with the specific rule failure recorded.


### Where can validated intake data be routed after extraction?


Validated records can be routed to Google Sheets for immediate visibility or to Snowflake for long-term structured storage and analytics. Routing logic can also branch based on document attributes, such as high-value claims going to senior reviewers or failed validations going to a triage queue.


### Can Jinba send emails or respond to customers automatically?


No. Jinba is designed for human-in-the-loop approval. It can draft responses, such as acknowledgement emails, but those drafts appear in a reviewer queue and are not sent until a named human reviews, edits if needed, and approves them.


### How does human-in-the-loop review work in Jinba?


When a workflow generates a draft outbound action, Jinba shows it as a card in the assigned reviewer's queue. The reviewer must approve or edit the draft before it is sent or finalized, so a human remains responsible for every communication and final record.


### What audit trail does Jinba create for automated document intake?


Every document processed through the workflow creates a step-by-step audit trail that records when the email was received, who sent it, which attachments were processed, what fields were extracted, how each validation rule evaluated, who was assigned, and what review actions were taken. This record is written as the workflow runs, not reconstructed later.


### How do I set up a Gmail intake workflow in Jinba?


Start by configuring the scheduled Gmail listing, then test it with a sample of real incoming documents. Next, define the fields needed in Reducto, add validation rules in Modules Checker V2, and connect the routing destination. Activate and test each step in sequence rather than enabling the full workflow at once.
